name: Indo-European Family

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Most Indo-European languages have grammatical gender (2–3 genders: masculine/feminine, or masculine/feminine/neuter). Some branches (e.g., modern English, Bengali, Persian) have lost grammatical gender. Gender triggers agreement on articles, adjectives, pronouns, and sometimes verbs. Genus-level cards specify exact gender systems for each branch.

linguisticChallenges.inflectionalMorphology: Indo-European languages are predominantly inflectional (fusional) — a single morpheme can encode multiple grammatical categories simultaneously (e.g., case + number + gender in a single suffix). The degree of inflection varies enormously, from minimal (English, Persian) to extensive (Sanskrit, Lithuanian, Russian).
linguisticChallenges.agreementSystems: Most members have agreement systems where adjectives, determiners, and/or verbs must agree with nouns in gender, number, and/or case. Failure to maintain agreement is a common MT error.
linguisticChallenges.diverseWordOrders: Word order varies significantly across branches: SVO (Romance, Germanic, Slavic), SOV (Indic, Iranian), VSO (Celtic, some archaic stages). Some branches have relatively free word order with pragmatic reordering (Slavic, Baltic).
linguisticChallenges.scriptDiversity: The family uses Latin, Cyrillic, Devanagari, Arabic, Armenian, Georgian, Greek, Bengali, Gujarati, Gurmukhi, and other scripts. Script-specific handling is critical — genus cards specify script requirements.

notes: Family card for Indo-European (~648 members). This is deliberately broad — most specific translation-relevant properties are defined at the genus level (genus-romance.json, genus-slavic.json, genus-germanic.json, genus-indic.json, genus-iranian.json, genus-celtic.json, etc.). Properties set to null here vary too much within the family to generalize.

regions.region: Europe, South Asia, Central Asia, Americas, Oceania
